claims.text: Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, Cr-Mn-Fe-Co, and Cr-Mn-Fe can be prepared as equiatomic, single-phase FCC alloys after thermomechanical processing.
Identical thermomechanical processing can produce similar grain sizes and textures across the three alloy systems.
The quinary alloy has enhanced mechanical strength relative to the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The quinary alloy has different strain-hardening behavior from the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The strength and strain-hardening differences arise synergistically from increased lattice distortion and a distinct state of chemical short-range order.
Adding the fifth element enhances local lattice distortions in the quinary alloy.
Adding the fifth element promotes distinct chemical short-range-order clusters in the quinary alloy.
Local lattice distortions create localized energy barriers to dislocation motion.
Chemical short-range-order clusters create localized energy barriers to dislocation motion.
The localized energy barriers impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases the yield strength of the quinary alloy relative to the lower-component alloys.
Impeded dislocation motion alters the strain-hardening behavior of the quinary alloy.
The quinary alloy will show a systematic increase in yield strength relative to both the quaternary and ternary alloys under matched test conditions.
The quinary alloy will show a modified strain-hardening regime relative to both lower-component alloys.
The mechanical-property differences will correlate with measurable indicators of lattice distortion and distinct short-range-order patterns.
XRD peak broadening and microstrain analysis can serve as indicators of lattice distortion in these alloys.
APT or SANS can detect and quantify chemical short-range-order characteristics in these alloys.
Matching grain size and texture allows observed mechanical differences to be attributed to atomic-scale phenomena rather than extrinsic microstructural variation.
